The Iceland scallop Chlamys islandica exhibits a relatively modest maximum shell size compared to some other large pectinids, with an ultimate shell height in the region of 11 centimeters [Li = 11 centimeters]. This asymptotic dimension, attained only after several years of slow growth in the cold waters it inhabits, places it at an intermediate position among commercially valuable scallop species. Field surveys conducted off the coast of Iceland have consistently confirmed that individuals rarely exceed this value, suggesting a strong physiological constraint on somatic growth that is likely linked to the energetic demands of reproduction and the low ambient temperatures typical of subarctic environments. The initial wet weight at birth for this species is estimated to be 0.00000018 grams [Wwb = 0.00000018 grams], a value derived from the diameter of the egg itself which measures approximately 70 micrometers. This minute mass, characteristic of broadcast-spawning bivalves, represents the entire endowment of organic reserves available to the lecithotrophic larva before it must initiate exogenous feeding. The energetic capital contained within this tiny egg determines the duration of the entirely yolk-dependent phase and sets a fundamental constraint on the early life history trajectory of the species, as the larva must develop the ciliary feeding apparatus before its finite reserves are exhausted.

At a sustained water temperature of 2 °C [T = 2 °C], the developing embryo completes its initial developmental program and hatches after a period of approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days], an interval that is substantially longer than hatching times reported for pectinids from warmer waters. This extended embryonic duration is consistent with the pronounced temperature dependence of metabolic and cleavage rates in marine invertebrates and represents a critical bottleneck in the early life cycle at high latitudes. Following hatching, the larva continues its planktonic existence as a free-swimming veliger, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to planktotrophic feeding. The lecithotrophic stage is thus relatively brief, constrained by the small initial egg mass of 0.00000018 grams [Wwb = 0.00000018 grams]. After this initial endotrophic phase, the larva must successfully capture phytoplankton cells using its velar cilia to fuel further growth and development. Under these same thermal conditions, the time since birth at metamorphosis is estimated to be 75 days . at a temperature of 2 °C [T = 2 °C]This protracted pre-settlement period is a direct consequence of the cold temperatures, which slow metabolic processes and decelerate the developmental progression from the trochophore through the veliger and pediveliger stages, ultimately delaying the acquisition of metamorphic competence compared to populations in warmer regimes.

Life span estimates for Chlamys islandica indicate a remarkably long-lived species, with a maximum longevity of approximately 23 years [am = approximately 23 years] recorded in populations inhabiting the stable, cold waters of the North Atlantic at 2 °C [T = 2 °C]. This exceptional longevity is among the highest reported for the Pectinidae and stands in stark contrast to the much shorter lifespans of many temperate and tropical scallop species, which rarely exceed 6 to 8 years. The physiological mechanisms underpinning this extended lifespan likely involve a reduced metabolic rate at low temperatures, which slows the accumulation of cellular oxidative damage and delays the onset of reproductive senescence. This strategy of slow growth and delayed reproduction is typical of organisms inhabiting energetically constrained, stable environments where resources are scarce but predictable. Shell growth continues throughout life, albeit at a declining rate as the animal ages, and growth rings on the valves provide reliable annual records that corroborate the longevity estimates. The combination of a long reproductive lifespan with relatively low annual fecundity per spawning event represents a bet-hedging strategy that buffers population recruitment against interannual variability in food supply and environmental conditions in the subarctic habitat.

Sexual maturation in the Iceland scallop occurs at a discrete developmental milestone defined by shell height. The shell height at puberty for this species is 2.45 centimeters [Lp = 2.45 centimeters], a threshold that individuals typically attain after several years of benthic growth following settlement. This size at maturity is relatively small compared to the ultimate shell height of 11 centimeters [Li = 11 centimeters], indicating that a substantial portion of the lifespan is dedicated to reproductive effort once the pubertal size threshold is crossed. The onset of gametogenesis at this size represents a critical physiological transition, as resources are redirected from somatic growth toward gonadal development. Measurements of gonad dry weight taken from individuals with a shell height of 6.7 centimeters and collected from waters at 2 °C [T = 2 °C] yielded a value of 4.5 grams , providing a quantitative benchmark for reproductive investment at a size well above the pubertal threshold. This substantial gonad mass indicates that once past the size of puberty, Chlamys islandica invests heavily in gamete production, likely producing large numbers of eggs during each annual spawning event, a pattern consistent with an r-selected reproductive strategy within a long-lived, slow-growing life history framework.

Comparative studies of pectinid life histories reveal how tightly the prolonged larval duration and delayed maturation of Chlamys islandica are coupled to its thermal environment. The 75-day time since birth at metamorphosis (75 days since birth)  under a temperature of 2 °C [T = 2 °C] represents a significant extension relative to related species inhabiting warmer waters; for instance, Pecten maximus undergoes metamorphosis in roughly 25 days at 13 °C. This temperature dependency is also evident in the brief age at birth of 8 days [ab = 8 days] observed at 2 °C [T = 2 °C], which is already four times longer than the 2-day hatching time reported for P. maximus at 18 °C. The low metabolic costs imposed by the cold environment likely contribute to the species' exceptional maximum lifespan of 23 years [am = 23 years] at 2 °C [T = 2 °C], as slow rates of cellular turnover reduce the accrual of physiological damage over time. The gonad dry weight of 4.5 grams  recorded at a shell height of 6.7 centimeters reflects the significant investment of surplus resources toward reproduction that becomes possible under this slow-paced life history, where individuals can afford to defer maturity until reaching a shell height at puberty of 2.45 centimeters [Lp = 2.45 centimeters] and still enjoy many years of annual spawning activity thereafter at a temperature of 2 °C [T = 2 °C].
